title: THE DAY GOD TREATED THE SINLESS SON AS THOUGH HE HAD LIVED YOUR LIFE
paragraphs: THE DAY GOD TREATED THE SINLESS SON AS THOUGH HE HAD LIVED YOUR LIFE

He never committed a single sin. Yet at the cross, He carried the guilt of sinners. And buried inside one sentence of Scripture is a truth so overwhelming that, once you understand it, you may never look at Jesus, your past, or the grace of God the same way again.
There is something about the cross that most people have heard about their entire lives… but have never truly understood.
And perhaps the most terrifying part is that we can become so familiar with the death of Jesus that we stop trembling at what actually happened there.
We wear crosses around our necks. We hang them on our walls. We post Bible verses about Calvary. We sing about the blood of Jesus.
But have you ever sat alone long enough to ask yourself one question?
What actually happened between the sinless Son of God and the Father when Jesus took the place of sinners?
Not merely what the Roman soldiers did to His body.
Not merely what the religious leaders did to His reputation.
But what happened when the One who had never sinned stood in the place of those who had?
Because there is one verse in the Bible that opens a window into the very heart of the Gospel.
And when you understand what the apostle Paul was saying, you begin to realize that the cross was not simply an innocent Man dying a terrible death.
It was the holy Son of God willingly bearing what guilty people deserved so that guilty people could be reconciled to a holy God.
And one of those guilty people…
Was me.
Was you.
Imagine that every secret you have ever buried suddenly becomes visible.
Every lie you told because the truth would have exposed you.
Every thought you entertained when nobody was watching.
Every person you wounded and never apologized to.
Every promise to God you broke.
Every moment when you knew what was right and deliberately chose what was wrong.
Not just the sins people discovered.
The ones they never discovered.
Imagine standing before a Judge who knows absolutely everything.
There is no clever explanation.
No edited testimony.
No comparison with someone worse than you.
Only truth.
And then imagine hearing that Someone who has never committed a single crime has willingly come forward to bear your penalty.
Not because you were innocent.
Not because your wrongdoing was insignificant.
But because He loved you.
Now listen carefully.
Even that illustration cannot fully capture the holiness of God, the seriousness of sin, or the wonder of Christ's sacrifice.
Because what happened at Calvary was infinitely greater than a courtroom exchange between two ordinary human beings.
The One who came to save us was the eternal Son of God.
And the One who needed saving was humanity, fallen in Adam, alienated by sin, and utterly unable to purchase its own redemption.
This is why 2 Corinthians 5:21 deserves more than a quick reading.
It deserves our attention.
Our tears.
Our repentance.
And our worship.
The King James Version records the words this way:
“For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.” — 2 Corinthians 5:21 (KJV)
Read it again.
Slowly.
God made Him who knew no sin to be sin for us.
How can the One who never sinned be made sin?
Did Jesus become morally corrupt?
Did He cease to be holy?
Did the Father transform His beloved Son into an actual sinner?
No.
And understanding why the answer is no is essential to understanding the Gospel itself.
The original Greek text reads:
Τὸν μὴ γνόντα ἁμαρτίαν ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν ἁμαρτίαν ἐποίησεν, ἵνα ἡμεῖς γενώμεθα δικαιοσύνη θεοῦ ἐν αὐτῷ.
A close English rendering is:
“He made the One who did not know sin to be sin on our behalf, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God.”
These are not ordinary words.
They are the language of reconciliation, substitution, grace, and a salvation no human being could ever earn.
And the first phrase already confronts us with something astonishing.
“The One who did not know sin.”
The Greek expression ton mē gnonta hamartian refers to One who did not know sin.
The word ginōskō, from which gnonta comes, can mean to know or experience.
Paul is not suggesting that Jesus lacked intellectual knowledge about sin.
Jesus knew exactly what sin was.
He exposed hypocrisy.
He confronted evil.
He recognized temptation.
He understood the human heart.
But He never committed sin.
Never.
Not once.
Think about that.
Jesus lived in a world filled with corruption without becoming corrupt.
He experienced hunger without surrendering to sinful discontent.
He experienced rejection without becoming vindictive.
He was falsely accused without becoming deceitful.
He was betrayed without becoming a betrayer.
He was tempted without yielding to temptation.
Hebrews 4:15 tells us that He was tempted as we are, yet without sin.
First Peter 2:22 declares that He committed no sin and that no deceit was found in His mouth.
First John 3:5 says that in Him there is no sin.
And Hebrews 7:26 describes our High Priest as holy, innocent, undefiled, and separated from sinners.
Do you understand what this means?
Jesus was not a slightly better version of humanity.
He was not merely the most disciplined religious teacher who ever lived.
He was the spotless Lamb of God.
The perfect Son.
Fully human, yet without sin.
Fully divine, worthy of eternal worship.
And that is precisely why His sacrifice could accomplish what ours never could.
Because sinners cannot save themselves by presenting their own righteousness to God.
We need a Savior who possesses the righteousness we lack.
Now comes the phrase that should stop us in our tracks.
“He made Him to be sin for us.”
The Greek word translated “sin” is hamartia.
Paul uses it twice in this verse.
The One who knew no hamartia was made hamartia for us.
Some readers encounter this language and assume it means Jesus became sinful in His nature.
But that interpretation contradicts the very first half of Paul's sentence, as well as the consistent witness of the New Testament.
Christ remained sinless.
His holiness was never corrupted.
His divine nature never changed.
The wonder is not that Jesus became evil.
The wonder is that the sinless One willingly bore the consequences of our evil.
In the immediate context, Paul is explaining how God reconciles sinners to Himself through Christ.
The language is profoundly substitutionary.
Jesus acted on our behalf.
The Greek phrase hyper hēmōn means “for us” or “on our behalf.”
And in this context, His death was not simply an example of courage.
It was a saving sacrifice.
Christ bore the judgment that sin deserved.
He did not become a sinner by personal wrongdoing.
He stood in the place of sinners as their representative and substitute.

Some interpreters also observe that the Greek word hamartia can carry the sense of “sin offering” in certain contexts of the Greek Old Testament. That background may illuminate Paul's sacrificial language, although scholars differ on whether “sin offering” is the best direct translation here.
What remains unmistakable is Paul's central claim.
The sinless Christ was given for sinners so that, in union with Him, sinners might receive the righteousness of God.
And here is where the story becomes painfully personal.
Because it is possible to admire the cross without admitting why we needed it.
We can sing about grace while secretly believing we are reasonably good people.
We can talk about forgiveness while refusing to confess our sins.
We can love the idea of heaven while resisting the Lordship of Jesus Christ.
But the cross will not allow us to pretend.
If our sin were a minor inconvenience, why would redemption require the death of the Son of God?
If human goodness could reconcile us to God, why would Christ need to suffer?
If religious activity could erase guilt, why would the spotless Lamb be offered?
The cross exposes the seriousness of our condition.
But it also reveals the immeasurable depth of God's love.
And that is the part I hope you never forget.
God did not wait for us to become worthy before sending His Son.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
While we were still sinners.
Not after we repaired everything.
Not after we learned how to pray beautifully.
Not after our addictions disappeared.
Not after our marriages healed.
Not after our secret habits stopped.
Not after our reputations improved.
While we were still sinners.
Christ died for us.
That does not mean God approves of sin.
It means His grace reaches sinners who cannot rescue themselves.
Perhaps you know what it feels like to be ashamed of your own story.
Perhaps you have done something you wish you could remove from history.
Perhaps you have spent years convincing people that you are fine while privately carrying a burden nobody sees.
You smile at church.
You say “God is good.”
You encourage other people.
But late at night, when the noise disappears, your conscience begins speaking.
You remember the betrayal.
The secret relationship.
The money you took.
The words you said.
The people you manipulated.
The bitterness you nurtured.
The years you wasted.
The person you used to be.
Or perhaps the person you are still struggling not to become.
And somewhere in the silence, a terrible question rises.
“After everything I have done, could God really forgive someone like me?”
That is not a small question.
For some people, it is the question that has haunted them for decades.
And the answer is not found in pretending that their sins were harmless.
It is found at Calvary.
Because the Gospel does not say your sins were too small to matter.
It says Christ's sacrifice is sufficient to save those who come to Him in faith.
Listen to the prophet Isaiah, writing centuries before the crucifixion.
In Isaiah 53:5–6, the King James Version says:
“But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.
All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned every one to his own way; and the LORD hath laid on him the iniquity of us all.”
The Hebrew text of Isaiah 53:6 contains these remarkable words:
וַיהוָה הִפְגִּיעַ בּוֹ אֵת עֲוֹן כֻּלָּנוּ
Va-Adonai hifgia bo et avon kullanu.
A close translation is:
“And the LORD caused the iniquity of us all to fall upon Him.”
The Hebrew word avon carries the sense of iniquity or guilt and, in some contexts, its consequences.
The verb hifgia here communicates the LORD's action in causing that iniquity to fall upon the suffering Servant.
Notice the direction of the action.
The iniquity belongs to us.
The suffering falls upon Him.
And the New Testament identifies Jesus Christ as the fulfillment of Isaiah's suffering Servant prophecy, as seen in Acts 8:32–35 and 1 Peter 2:24–25.
This is not a story about God overlooking evil.
It is a story about God dealing with sin through the self-giving sacrifice of His Son.
And we must be careful here.
The Father did not force an unwilling Jesus into a tragedy He wanted to escape.
Jesus willingly laid down His life.
In John 10:18, He said:
“No man taketh it from me, but I lay it down of myself.”
The cross was not an accident.
It was not God's desperate attempt to recover from a failed plan.
It was the fulfillment of His saving purpose.
The Father sent the Son.
The Son willingly gave Himself.
And through the eternal Spirit, Christ offered Himself without spot to God, as Hebrews 9:14 teaches.
The work of redemption reveals the united purpose of the triune God.
Now imagine the scene.
Jerusalem.
A hill outside the city.
The air heavy with dust.
Soldiers standing near the crosses.
Religious leaders watching.
Passersby mocking.
Women grieving.
A mother looking upon the suffering of her Son.
And in the center of it all…
Jesus.
The One who touched lepers without becoming unclean.
The One who welcomed children when others considered them interruptions.
The One who forgave sinners who had nowhere else to go.
The One who commanded storms to be still.
The One who called Lazarus out of the tomb.
Now hanging upon a Roman cross.
His hands pierced.
His body wounded.
His enemies mocking.
And yet His suffering was not merely the physical pain of crucifixion.
Scripture reveals that He was bearing our sins.
First Peter 2:24 says:
“Who his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree, that we, being dead to sins, should live unto righteousness: by whose stripes ye were healed.”
Our sins.
Not His.
Our guilt.
Not His.
Our need for reconciliation.
Not His.
And then, from the cross, Jesus cried out:
“Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani?”
Matthew 27:46 preserves this cry in a Semitic form and translates it:
“My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?”
The words echo the opening of Psalm 22.
This is sacred ground, and we should not pretend to understand every mystery of what Christ experienced in His suffering.
Scripture does not teach that the Trinity was broken apart or that the Son ceased to be God.
Nor should we imagine that the Father stopped loving the Son.
Yet Jesus truly entered the depths of suffering and abandonment expressed in that lament, as He bore sin in His saving death.
His cry was real.
His anguish was real.
His sacrifice was real.
And the psalm He quoted does not end in despair.
Psalm 22 moves from suffering toward vindication and worldwide praise.
The crucifixion was not the final chapter.
But before we reach the empty tomb, we need to understand one more phrase in Paul's astonishing verse.
“That we might be made the righteousness of God in Him.”
This is where the Gospel becomes almost too beautiful for words.
Because Paul does not merely say that Christ died so we could feel less guilty.
He does not merely say that Jesus came to improve our self-esteem.
He says that God's saving purpose was that we might become the righteousness of God in Him.
The Greek expression is:
ἵνα ἡμεῖς γενώμεθα δικαιοσύνη θεοῦ ἐν αὐτῷ
Hina hēmeis genōmetha dikaiosynē theou en autō.
“So that we might become the righteousness of God in Him.”
The word dikaiosynē means righteousness.
And the final words, en autō, mean “in Him.”
Do not overlook those two words.
In Him.
Not in our accomplishments.
Not in our religious performance.
Not in our family background.
Not in our reputation.
In Christ.

Christian interpreters have discussed the precise nuance of “become the righteousness of God.” Many emphasize the righteous standing believers receive through Christ; others also highlight how believers become living witnesses to God's reconciling righteousness. These emphases need not erase the verse's unmistakable center: our reconciliation and new standing before God are found in Christ, not in self-earned merit.
Paul explains elsewhere, in Philippians 3:9, that the righteousness he seeks is not his own righteousness derived from the law, but righteousness through faith in Christ.
And Romans 3:23–24 declares:
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God;
Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.”
Freely.
By grace.
Through Christ.
Do you see the beauty?
The Gospel is not a message telling guilty people to manufacture enough goodness to make God accept them.
It is the announcement that God has acted in Jesus Christ to reconcile sinners to Himself.
And this reconciliation is received through faith.
Not purchased.
Not negotiated.
Not inherited from religious parents.
Not earned by donations.
Not secured by church attendance.
Received through Christ.
This is why the cross is so offensive to human pride.
It tells the respectable religious person, “You cannot save yourself.”
And it tells the disgraced sinner, “You are not beyond the reach of Christ's saving grace.”
The proud must come down.
The broken may come near.
And both must come through Jesus.
But perhaps you are wondering something.
“If Jesus has already paid the price, does that mean I can continue living however I want?”
Paul anticipated that kind of thinking.
In Romans 6:1–2, he asked whether believers should continue in sin so grace may abound.
His answer was emphatic.
“God forbid.”
Grace is not permission to cherish the sin that nailed our Savior to the cross.
Grace is the power of God bringing us out of sin's dominion and into new life.
Christ did not die merely to leave us comfortable in our chains.
He died to redeem us.
To reconcile us.
To make us His own.
To lead us into holiness.
Second Corinthians 5:15 says that Christ died for all so that those who live should no longer live for themselves, but for Him who died and rose again.
That is the transformation at the heart of the Gospel.
Not perfection manufactured overnight.
Not a performance designed to impress other Christians.
But a new direction.
A surrendered heart.
A life increasingly shaped by the Savior.
There will still be battles.
There may still be tears.
There will be moments when you stumble and must confess your sin.
But the person who belongs to Christ is no longer called to make peace with darkness.
You are called to walk in the light.
And if you fall, do not run farther into hiding.
Run to the Savior.
First John 1:9 tells believers that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse us.
And First John 2:1 reminds us that we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous.
Think about that.
The One who died for sinners is also the risen Advocate of those who belong to Him.
Your hope is not that you will never need mercy again.
Your hope is that Jesus Christ is a sufficient Savior.
Maybe someone reading this has been away from God for years.
You used to pray.
You used to open your Bible with hunger.
You used to care deeply about holiness.
But slowly, almost without noticing, other things became more important.
You became busy.
Then distracted.
Then spiritually numb.
And eventually you learned how to live without much prayer at all.
You still believe in God.
But you know something has changed.
You have grown accustomed to a distance that once would have broken your heart.
And now you are reading about the cross.
About the sinless Christ.
About the Savior who bore sin for people who could never save themselves.
And perhaps there is a quiet conviction rising inside you.
Not merely fear of consequences.
But sorrow that you have treated such costly grace so casually.
If that is you, do not harden your heart.
The call of the Gospel is not to hide your condition behind religious language.
It is to repent and believe.
To turn from sin and return to Christ.
To stop defending what God is calling you to surrender.
Because repentance is not the enemy of grace.
Repentance is a fitting response to the grace that calls us home.
And there is another person I want to speak to.
The one who has already repented but still cannot forgive themselves.
You know the Scriptures.
You believe Jesus died for sinners.
You have confessed what you did.
But you keep reopening the case against yourself.
Every time you begin to experience joy, your past interrupts.
Every time someone tells you that God loves you, you remember what you did.
And you quietly wonder whether peace is something other Christians are allowed to experience, but not you.
Listen.
The cross does not erase the reality of what happened.
Repentance may still require confession to those you harmed, restitution where appropriate, accepting consequences, and seeking to repair what can be repaired.
Grace is not a license to evade responsibility.
But neither does Scripture call the repentant believer to live forever as though Christ's sacrifice were insufficient.
Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.”
No condemnation in Christ does not mean your sin was imaginary. It means your Savior is sufficient.
You may still grieve what happened.
You may still have consequences to face.
You may still need time, counsel, and the patient work of healing.
But if you belong to Christ, your past is not your final identity.
The cross speaks a greater word.
And the resurrection confirms that death did not defeat Him.
On the third day, Jesus rose.
Not as a metaphor.
Not merely as a beautiful idea about hope.
But as the risen Lord, proclaimed by His apostles as the One whom God raised from the dead.
First Corinthians 15:3–4 summarizes the apostolic Gospel: Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, was buried, and rose again the third day according to the Scriptures.
The cross and resurrection belong together.
Without the cross, we do not understand the cost of redemption.
Without the resurrection, we do not have the triumphant announcement of the living Savior.
But together they proclaim the message that has changed lives across centuries.
Sin is serious.
Grace is real.
Christ is risen.
And sinners are called to come to Him.
That is why our Gospel Warrior message has always centered on this truth:
Not because every scandal disappears from human memory.
Not because consequences always vanish.
Not because following Jesus guarantees an easy life.
But because the Gospel can give a new identity, a new allegiance, a new hope, and a new future to people whose stories seemed ruined by sin.
Consider Peter.
He denied knowing Jesus.
Three times.
At the very moment when courage was needed, fear overcame him.
And when the rooster crowed, Peter wept bitterly.
Yet the risen Jesus restored him and entrusted him with the care of His sheep.
Consider Paul.
Before he became an apostle, he persecuted the church.
He later described himself as a blasphemer, persecutor, and violent man who had received mercy.
Consider the dying criminal beside Jesus.
He had no opportunity to build an impressive religious résumé.
Yet he turned to Christ in faith, and Jesus promised him paradise.
These stories are not proof that sin is harmless.
They are proof that the mercy of Christ is astonishing.
And maybe your own story is not finished either.
Maybe the chapter you thought was the ending is the very place where God is calling you to surrender.
Maybe the tears you have been hiding are the beginning of an honest prayer.
Maybe the person who feels least worthy of God's attention needs to hear that salvation has never been a reward for the worthy.
It is grace for sinners through Jesus Christ.
But please understand something.
No article can repent for you.
No emotional moment can substitute for genuine faith.
Only Jesus saves.
And His invitation stands.
Second Corinthians 5:20, the verse immediately before our central passage, says:
“Now then we are ambassadors for Christ, as though God did beseech you by us: we pray you in Christ's stead, be ye reconciled to God.”
Be reconciled to God.
That is the invitation.
Not merely to become more religious.
Not merely to feel inspired for a few minutes.
But to be reconciled to the living God through Jesus Christ.
If your heart is convicted right now, you can speak to Him where you are.
You do not need impressive words.
You do not need to pretend.
You can pray something like this:

“Lord Jesus, I have sinned against You. I cannot make myself righteous. I believe You are the sinless Son of God who died for sinners and rose again. I turn from my sin and place my trust in You. Forgive me, change my heart, teach me to follow You, and make my life belong to You. Thank You for Your mercy. Amen.”
A prayer is not a magic formula.
Our confidence rests in Jesus Christ, not in the perfection of our words.
But if that prayer expresses your sincere repentance and faith, do not treat this moment as the end of your journey.
Begin walking with Him.
Open the Scriptures.
Find a faithful local church where the Gospel is preached and disciples are nurtured.
Seek baptism and Christian fellowship in obedience to His Word.
Learn to pray even when the words come slowly.
And when you stumble, return to the truth of the Gospel.
Because the Christian life is not sustained by yesterday's emotional experience.
It is sustained by the living Christ.
And this is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not simply to publish another inspirational message.
Not to entertain people with religious language.
But to keep pointing wounded hearts, wandering believers, searching souls, and struggling families back to the truth of God's Word.
Every article is an opportunity for someone to encounter Scripture.
Every shared testimony can remind a struggling believer that they are not alone.
Every invitation to read the Bible can become the beginning of deeper discipleship.
And every person who chooses to help spread the Gospel participates in work that can bless people they may never meet.
Perhaps you have been encouraged by these messages.
Perhaps a Scripture we shared reached you during a night when you were spiritually exhausted.
Perhaps you have quietly read Gospel Warrior posts for months without ever commenting.
If so, I want to invite you to do something meaningful today.
Not because we need to manufacture an emotional response.
But because honest testimonies can encourage other people to seek Christ.
Or if you are exhausted from pretending everything is fine, simply comment, “Pray for me.”
You do not have to expose private details publicly.
And if you are ready to tell part of your testimony, share what the Lord has been teaching you about forgiveness, repentance, or surrender.
Someone reading the comments may be struggling with the very same questions.
Your words could help them realize that they are not alone in seeking God's mercy.
And please do not let this message end with you.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God.
But because the person scrolling through your feed may need to hear the Gospel.
A family member who has drifted away from church.
A friend who feels condemned by their past.
A young believer fighting temptation.
A parent praying for a wayward child.
Or someone who has never understood why Jesus died.
You may not know what someone is carrying.
You may never know whether they read every word.
But you can faithfully place the truth of Scripture before them.
We also want to help you go deeper than a single post.
These resources are offered to encourage Bible reading, spiritual growth, prayer, and faithful discipleship.
And if this ministry has become part of your spiritual encouragement, I would like to extend a personal invitation.

It is a voluntary way to help sustain and expand the ministry's ongoing work of sharing biblical teaching, encouraging struggling believers, and making Gospel-centered resources available to more people.
But I want to be very clear about something because the Gospel we preach requires it.
The New Testament teaches that Christian giving should be willing, thoughtful, and cheerful, not driven by pressure or compulsion (2 Corinthians 9:7).
Your responsibilities to your family, your local church, and those in genuine need matter.
It can help us keep creating, teaching, encouraging, and reaching more people with the message of Christ.
These items are simply expressions of gratitude and opportunities to keep biblical encouragement close in everyday life.
They are not the reason we proclaim the Gospel.
Jesus is.
You are welcome here.
Because the Gospel is not merchandise.
Grace is not for sale.
And the blood of Jesus is not a product anyone can purchase.
The invitation to eternal life remains exactly what Scripture declares it to be.
The gift of God through Jesus Christ our Lord.
Now, before you leave, I want to return to the verse where we began.
“For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.”
Do you hear it differently now?
He knew no sin.
Yet He gave Himself for sinners.
He owed no debt of guilt.
Yet He bore our sins.
He deserved no condemnation.
Yet He suffered in our place.
And through Him, those who repent and believe are welcomed into reconciliation with God.
The cross was not merely a public execution.
It was the place where the holy love and justice of God were displayed in the saving sacrifice of Christ.
And the empty tomb announces that the crucified Savior lives.
So when your past tells you that you are beyond forgiveness, remember Christ.
When pride tells you that you are good enough without Him, remember Christ.
When temptation tells you that sin is harmless, remember Christ.
When suffering makes you wonder whether God understands pain, remember Christ.
And when the enemy of your soul tries to convince you that your story can never change, remember the apostle's words.
“In Him.”
That is where our hope lives.
Not in who we were.
Not in what we have achieved.
Not in the applause of the world.
In Jesus Christ.
The One who knew no sin.
The One who died for sinners.
The One who rose from the grave.
The One who still calls people to repentance and faith.
If this truth has reached a place in your heart that you have kept hidden for years, do not dismiss it as another passing feeling.
Bring that place into the light before God.
And if you have never truly surrendered your life to Jesus, do not confuse knowing about His cross with personally trusting the Savior who died there.
Come to Him.
While you have breath.
While His Word is before you.
While the invitation of the Gospel is being proclaimed.
Because the deepest question is not simply whether you understand the Greek of 2 Corinthians 5:21.
It is whether you have entrusted your life to the Christ whom that verse proclaims.
One day, every earthly achievement will seem small.
Every social media argument will fall silent.
Every title and possession will lose its power to impress.
And what will matter eternally is whether we belong to Jesus Christ.
So do not merely admire His sacrifice.
Trust Him.
Follow Him.
Worship Him.
And let the grace that saves you also teach you to live for the One who gave Himself for you.
The most astonishing thing about your story is not how far you fell, but how far the sinless Savior was willing to go to redeem sinners like you and me.
